Text: Food Jars — specs, MOQ and documents | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Guides / Food Jars Guide Food Jars: Wide Mouth, Tamper Evidence and the Filling Problem By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou · Updated 26 October 2026 A food jar is chosen by the filling line before the shelf: how wide the mouth is decides how fast you can fill, and how you close it decides whether the customer trusts it. Food jars look simple and are decided by three things: the mouth diameter, the closure, and whether the product is hot or cold when it goes in. Get those right and the rest is decoration. We mould 250 ml and 500 ml PET food jars with 63 mm and 70 mm mouths, and quote PP where hot filling or chemical resistance demands it. Check it before you quote The free Bottle Spec Checker tests whether your neck fits the closure and whether the wall survives a pump stroke. 30-second check: does your bottle pass? Open ▾ Capacity (ml) Wall (mm) Closure Lotion pump Sprayer Flip-top Dropper Screw cap Full Check → — Wide Mouth vs Narrow Mouth A wide mouth fills faster and takes a spoon; a narrow mouth pours. For spices and powders, wide mouth with a sifter insert; for honey and sauces, narrow with a controlled-flow cap. The mouth also sets the tamper-evident options: induction seal liners need a flat land on the rim, and not every jar design has one. Hot Fill and Why PET Has a Ceiling Standard PET softens above roughly 60 °C. For jams and sauces filled hot, PP is the safer material and the lower in unit cost answer overall — even though the jar looks less premium in clear. We would rather quote PP and keep the line running than sell a PET jar that distorts on your filler. Tamper Evidence That Actually Gets Used Induction seal liners are the default for food: they leave a visible membrane and are obvious if broken. Pressure-sensitive liners are easier to apply but easier to reseal unnoticed. For export markets where the retailer audits the pack, induction is the safer conversation. Where Food Jars Fail Food packaging failures are seal failures, not shape failures. Three to check before the carton is printed. Induction Seal Needs a Flat Land The foil seals to a flat rim. A decorative rim with a 1 mm land will not hold, and no torque fixes it. Check the rim width on the drawing. Hot Fill Distorts Standard PET Above roughly 60 °C, standard PET deforms. For jam and sauces we quote PP, even though clear PET looks better on shelf. Vacuum Pull on Cooling A hot-filled jar cools and pulls a vacuum; a thin wall collapses inward. PP with a thicker wall handles it, PET does not. What Documents a Food Buyer Should Ask For The resin declaration of compliance, and a migration test on the finished article where the destination market requires it. For export to the EU, the declaration must reference EU 10/2011 and the specific monomer limits. Ask per batch, not per product family — the resin lot is what the declaration covers. Questions We Get on This Are your food jars food-contact certified? The PET grades carry an EU 10/2011 declaration per order; we hold a migration test on PE grades and a RoHS verification. Ask for the document that matches the exact grade you buy. Can I put jam in a PET jar? Only if it is filled cold. Hot jam above about 60 °C needs PP, or a heat-set PET we do not offer. Do you supply the lid with the jar? Yes — screw caps, induction liners and sifter inserts, matched to the mouth. Can the jar be square instead of round? Square footprints stack better and are available in the 500 ml size; round is standard for 250 ml. Can PET jars be used for hot fill? No for standard PET above about 60 °C. PP or heat-set PET is the answer. Do you supply induction seal liners? Yes where the rim has a flat land wide enough for the seal. What MOQ applies to food jars? 1,000 pcs per colour on stock moulds. Text: Hand Soap Bottles — specs, MOQ and documents | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Guides / Hand Soap Bottles Guide Hand Soap Bottles: Why 250 ml Is the Most Repeat-Ordered Size By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou · Updated 26 October 2026 Hand soap is the one bottle a household buys again without thinking. That makes it the most repeat-ordered SKU in the category — and the one where a pump that fails after 200 strokes costs you the account. Hand soap and hand wash sell in 250, 300 and 500 ml, in clear PET or opaque HDPE, with a lotion pump or a foaming pump. The bottle is commodity; the pump is where returns come from. This page covers the sizes we mould, the difference between a lotion pump and a foaming pump, and what to specify so the third refill still works. Check it before you quote The free Bottle Spec Checker tests whether your neck fits the closure and whether the wall survives a pump stroke. 30-second check: does your bottle pass? Open ▾ Capacity (ml) Wall (mm) Closure Lotion pump Sprayer Flip-top Dropper Screw cap Full Check → — Lotion Pump vs Foaming Pump A lotion pump pushes product up the dip tube and out through a nozzle. A foaming pump mixes air with liquid at the nozzle and needs a low-viscosity formula plus a foaming agent — you cannot put a thick gel in a foamer. The necks are the same 24/410 or 28/410, so the bottle does not change; the pump does. That is why the same 250 ml mould serves both product types. 250 ml Is a Repeat Purchase, Not a Premium One A 250 ml hand soap is bought every six to eight weeks by the same household. The pack has to look consistent on shelf over years, which makes colour matching more important than novelty. For private label, the same bottle runs in white, cream and clear for different retailers — three colours, one mould, 1,000 pcs each. What Makes a Pump Fail In practice, three things: a dip tube that does not reach the bottom (product left behind), a spring that corrodes with a high-salt formula, and a neck thread that is not tight enough to hold the pump under repeated strokes. We test the pump on the bottle, filled, for a cycle count agreed with the closure supplier before the order ships. If your formula is high-salt or high-alcohol, say so — the spring material changes. Labels in a Wet Bathroom Hand soap lives next to a tap. Paper labels wrinkle and permanent adhesive lifts at the edges after a few weeks of steam. Specify a synthetic label with a waterproof adhesive, or print directly on the bottle. Silkscreen is the lowest unit cost durable option at 1,000 pcs; it also avoids the label edge that collects water. Where Hand Soap Bottles Fail Hand soap is replaced every few weeks, so the pack has to survive dozens of refills. Three failures. Pump Corrodes With a High-Salt Formula Sanitiser and salt-based soaps attack the spring. Specify the spring material with the formula, not after the first complaint. Thread Loosens Over Refills A pump re-screwed 20 times wears the thread. A slightly deeper thread on the neck costs nothing at mould stage. Label Edge Collects Residue Soap residue builds on the label edge. Silkscreen has no edge; a synthetic label with rounded corners reduces it. 250 ml vs 500 ml for Commercial Buyers 250 ml is the household size; 500 ml is the washroom and HoReCa size. The 500 ml must take a lockable pump for refill carts, which is a closure decision rather than a bottle one. Questions We Get on This What is the most common hand soap bottle size? 250 ml for consumer hand wash; 300–500 ml for refill and family formats. 500 ml is also the standard for commercial washrooms. Can I use a foaming pump on any bottle? Yes if the neck matches and the formula is thin enough. A foaming pump will not work with a thick gel — it needs a low-viscosity soap with a foaming agent. Choosing the neck first cuts the range to two or three options, and the rest is dose, finish and liner. The failure we see most is a seal that does not bond because the rim land is not flat. Text: Lotion Bottles — specs, MOQ and documents | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Guides / Lotion Bottles Guide Lotion Bottles: Why 300 ml Is the Size Where the Pump Decides the Feel By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou · Updated 26 October 2026 Body lotion is judged twice: on shelf by the bottle, in the hand by the pump. At 300 ml the two are almost the same decision — the wall thickness and the pump output together decide whether it feels low-cost. Body lotion sells in 200, 250, 300 and 500 ml. The 300 ml is the retail standard in Europe and Asia: large enough to feel like value, small enough to sit on a shelf next to a shower gel. This page covers what changes between those sizes, and why the pump — not the bottle — is usually what a customer remembers. Check it before you quote The free Bottle Spec Checker tests whether your neck fits the closure and whether the wall survives a pump stroke. 30-second check: does your bottle pass? Open ▾ Capacity (ml) Wall (mm) Closure Lotion pump Sprayer Flip-top Dropper Screw cap Full Check → — Dose per Stroke Is a Product Decision A 1.2 ml stroke is right for a face lotion; a 2.0 ml stroke suits a body lotion that people use generously. The bottle is the same 300 ml mould — the pump changes the experience more than the shape does. If the lotion is thick, a wider dip tube and a larger valve prevent the “pumping air” feeling at the end of the bottle. That is worth specifying before the artwork. Why 300 ml Feels Premium and 500 ml Feels Economical At 300 ml the bottle fits one hand; at 500 ml it needs two. That is the whole difference in perceived quality, and it has nothing to do with the plastic. Wall thickness matters at both sizes: 0.55 mm reads fine on a 300 ml, but on a 500 ml the same wall can flex under a full pump stroke. PET or HDPE for Lotion Clear PET shows the emulsion and supports a “clean” positioning; HDPE is opaque, it costs less per gram and hides the fill level as the bottle empties — which is why value lines and professional sizes use it. If the formula contains a solvent or a high level of essential oil, check the inner compatibility before choosing PET; some oils craze the surface over months. Decoration That Survives a Bathroom Shelf A lotion bottle lives in humidity. Paper labels wrinkle; permanent adhesive lifts. Silkscreen and spray-coat finishes are the durable options, and both start at 1,000 pcs (spray coat at 3,000). For a 300 ml line with three SKUs, the usual setup is the same bottle, three colours and one pump type — costs less than three different moulds, and easier to keep on shelf together. Where Lotion Bottles Fail Body lotion is judged in the hand, and three things ruin that judgement. Pump Stroke Too Small for the Body A 1.2 ml stroke on a 300 ml body lotion means eight pumps per leg. A 2.0 ml stroke is the difference between 'rich' and 'stingy'. Wall Too Thin for a Full Bottle A full 500 ml at 0.55 mm flexes on a one-handed pump. 0.65 mm holds. Dip Tube Too Short The last 20-30 ml is unreachable. Cut the tube to the base curve, not to the shoulder. Why 300 ml Reads Premium A 300 ml fits one hand, a 500 ml needs two. That is the whole difference in perceived quality, and it has nothing to do with the plastic. Questions We Get on This What is the standard body lotion bottle size? 300 ml in Europe and Asia; 500 ml for value and family sizes; 200–250 ml for travel and gift sets. Which pump suits a thick lotion? A 2.0 ml stroke pump with a wider dip tube. A standard 1.2 ml pump will feel like it is straining. Can the same bottle be used for lotion and hand soap? Yes — the 24/410 neck takes both pumps. Only the pump and the label change. Do you supply the pump with the bottle? Yes, 24/410 and 28/410 lotion pumps, fitted and tested before packing. What is the standard body lotion size? 300 ml in Europe and Asia, 500 ml for value and family sizes. Can one bottle serve lotion and hand soap?

## https://8pck.com/guides/pet-bottles/
Title: PET Bottles — specs, MOQ and documents | 8PCK
Description: PET is the default clear plastic bottle for cosmetics, personal care and food. It is also the material most often specified without a grade — which is wher
Sections: PET vs HDPE vs PETG; What “rPET” Means on a Purchase Order; Food Contact and the Documents That Matter; When PET Is the Wrong Choice; Where PET Fails, and How to See It Coming; Recycled Content: What a Supplier Should Be Able to Say; Questions We Get on This; Sizes That Fit This Guide
Text: PET Bottles — specs, MOQ and documents | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Guides / PET Bottles Guide PET Bottles: Grades, Clarity, and When PET Is the Wrong Choice By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou · Updated 26 October 2026 PET is the default clear plastic bottle for cosmetics, personal care and food. It is also the material most often specified without a grade — which is where clarity, weight and cost problems start. Polyethylene terephthalate — PET — is chosen for three properties: it is clear, it is stiff enough to hold a pump without flexing, and it takes decoration well. It is not the least expensive resin, and it is not the right choice for every product. This page covers the grades we run, how PET compares with HDPE and PETG, what recycled content actually means on a purchase order, and the cases where we steer customers away from it. Check it before you quote The free Bottle Spec Checker tests whether your neck fits the closure and whether the wall survives a pump stroke. 30-second check: does your bottle pass? Open ▾ Capacity (ml) Wall (mm) Closure Lotion pump Sprayer Flip-top Dropper Screw cap Full Check → — PET vs HDPE vs PETG PET is clear and stiff. HDPE is opaque, softer, and it costs less per gram — it is what you use for shampoo and detergent where the product does not need to be seen. PETG sits between: clearer than HDPE, thicker-walled than PET, and the usual choice for airless packs and premium thick-wall cosmetic bottles. The practical rule: if the bottle has to sell the product on shelf, PET or PETG. If it has to survive a rough supply chain at the lowest unit cost, HDPE. What “rPET” Means on a Purchase Order Recycled content is a percentage, not a yes/no. rPET at 30% behaves almost identically to virgin PET; at 70–100% the colour shifts slightly warmer and the food-contact documentation changes. If your customer needs a recycled-content claim, ask for the percentage on the declaration and confirm which grade it applies to — a generic “eco bottle” line on a website is not a document anyone can audit. Food Contact and the Documents That Matter For food and beverage contact, the relevant framework in the EU is Regulation 10/2011 with the declaration of compliance from the resin supplier, plus migration testing on the finished article. We hold an EU 10/2011 + 1935/2004 overall migration test on PE grades and a RoHS verification. PET and PETG declarations are issued per order against the resin supplier's DoC — we do not claim a test we have not run. When PET Is the Wrong Choice Hot filling above roughly 60 °C will distort a standard PET bottle unless it is heat-set, which we do not offer. Aggressive solvents — some essential oils, some industrial chemicals — can craze or stress-crack PET. And very large formats above 1 L are usually better in HDPE for cost and drop resistance. Where PET Fails, and How to See It Coming PET is a good material with three specific weaknesses. Each shows up in a testable window. Crazing With Alcohol or Essential Oil Fine surface cracks appear at the shoulder after weeks, not days. A four-week soak of a filled sample catches it; a compatibility table does not. Distortion Above 60 °C Standard PET deforms in a hot-fill line or a hot container. Heat-set PET exists but is a different mould and 20-30 % more expensive. Stress Cracking at the Base Thin bases crack when a full bottle is dropped on a corner. A 0.5 mm base on a 500 ml is the practical floor for a pump-fitted bottle. Recycled Content: What a Supplier Should Be Able to Say If the pack carries a recycled claim, the supplier should name the grade and the percentage, state whether it is physical or mass-balance recycled, and provide the declaration per batch. Higher rPET content shifts clear PET slightly warmer — fine for amber, green and coloured packs, awkward for water-clear. Questions We Get on This Is PET food safe? Get the neck wrong and the pump leaks; get the wall thickness wrong and the bottle collapses under a full stroke. This guide covers the sizes we mould, the necks they take, the pumps that fit, and the four numbers that settle a brief. Pump bottles are the default pack for anything dispensed by the stroke: hand soap, body wash, shampoo, lotion, sanitiser, pet shampoo. The category looks simple and is not, because the bottle and the pump are made by different processes and still have to fit together at speed on a filling line. We blow the bottle and injection-mould the pump and cap in the same building. That matters more than it sounds: a pump that fits our bottle is tested on our bottle, not on a drawing. Check it before you quote The free Bottle Spec Checker tests whether your neck fits the closure and whether the wall survives a pump stroke. 30-second check: does your bottle pass? Open ▾ Capacity (ml) Wall (mm) Closure Lotion pump Sprayer Flip-top Dropper Screw cap Full Check → — The Three Parts, and Which One Actually Fails Almost every complaint about a pump bottle traces to one of three interfaces: the pump against the neck, the dip tube against the base, or the shoulder against the stroke. Each has a different fix. The Bottle The bottle provides stiffness, not strength. A 500 ml PET at 28 g holds its shape under a full stroke; the same mould run at 22 g flexes at the shoulder and draws air back through the pump. This is why weight is quoted with the mould rather than negotiated after the sample: drop below the wall the mould was cut for and the pump starts to gulp. The Neck A 24/410 pump on a 24/415 bottle threads on and leaks. The difference is 2.5 mm of thread height, which is invisible on a photo and obvious on a filling line. If you already buy closures, send one. We test it on the bottle before quoting rather than assuming the neck is standard — it usually is, and occasionally it is not. The Pump Three failure modes dominate: a spring that corrodes with a high-salt formula, a valve that clogs with a particulate gel, and an actuator too small for the viscosity, which feels stiff after the first hundred strokes. All three are testable in a week. None are fixable after the container ships. Sizes and Which Markets Buy Them Nominal capacity is measured to the shoulder. With the pump inserted, usable fill is typically 5–8 % lower — a 500 ml bottle holds about 470–490 ml. Check the label claim against usable volume, not nominal. When 750 ml Pays Only with a 28/410 pump and a wall of at least 0.65 mm on the shoulder. Below that, the bottle flexes and the pump draws air for the last fifth of the fill. Wall Thickness, Weight and Where the Cost Sits Resin is bought by the tonne, so weight is the first cost lever and the last one most brands look at. A 500 ml PET at 28 g and one at 36 g look identical on a shelf and differ by roughly 25 % in material cost. The trap is cutting weight without re-testing the pump. Title: How to request a quote that comes back in one day | 8PCK
Description: Most quotes are slow because the brief is incomplete, not because the factory is slow. These are the six fields that turn an enquiry into a price.
Sections: The Six Fields; Why Each One Moves the Price; What Makes a Quote Slow; Stock or New Mould — Ask This First; What You Get Back; Two Things to Send With the Brief; The Five-Line Format We Use; After the Quote, the Four Steps That Matter
Text: How to request a quote that comes back in one day | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Guides / How to Request a Bottle Quote That Comes Back in One Day | 8PCK Guide How to Request a Quote That Comes Back in One Day By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou · Updated 31 October 2026 Most quotes are slow because the brief is incomplete, not because the factory is slow. These are the six fields that turn an enquiry into a price. A quote is an answer to a question. If the question is 'how much for bottles', the answer is a range; if the question names the capacity, the neck, the material, the decoration and the quantity, the answer can be a price. This page is the checklist we use internally. Send the same six lines and you will usually have a written quote within one business day — and a quote that does not move afterwards. Check it before you quote The free Bottle Spec Checker tests whether your neck fits the closure and whether the wall survives a pump stroke. 30-second check: does your bottle pass? Open ▾ Capacity (ml) Wall (mm) Closure Lotion pump Sprayer Flip-top Dropper Screw cap Full Check → — The Six Fields Capacity and shape — 250 ml Boston round, 30 ml dropper, 200 ml jar. A photo of a similar pack is acceptable and often faster. Neck finish — 24/410, 28/410, 20/410, 38 mm. If you do not know it, send the closure you intend to use and we measure it. Material — PET, HDPE, PETG, PP. If the formula is not water-based, say so; that changes the resin before it changes the price. Decoration — silkscreen, label, spray coat, metallising, hot stamp, or none. Each has its own MOQ and lead time. Quantity — the first run, and the annual volume if you know it. The first run sets the MOQ question; the annual volume sets the cavity count. Destination and terms — port or door, and whether the order ships filled or empty. Freight is part of the landed cost and changes the recommendation. Why Each One Moves the Price Capacity and material set the resin weight, which is the largest single line in a bottle's cost. A 500 ml PET at 28 g and the same bottle at 22 g differ by about 20 % on material alone. The neck decides which closures can be fitted, and a non-standard neck can mean a new insert rather than a stock mould. Decoration is where a cheap bottle becomes an expensive pack: four-colour silkscreen needs four screens, and metallising adds days and a rejection rate. Quantity changes the answer more than anything else: 1,000 pcs on a stock mould is a different product from 50,000 pcs with a dedicated run. What Makes a Quote Slow Nine times out of ten it is one missing field. The most common is the neck, followed by the quantity. The next most common is a reference to a pack the buyer saw online without a link. The second cause is a drawing without a closure. We can quote the bottle, but the moment the closure matters — and it usually does — the bottle price alone is not useful. The third is a formula question that arrives with the enquiry: 'will PET hold a 30 % alcohol gel'. That is a compatibility question, not a price question, and it needs a different answer (see the formula page). Stock or New Mould — Ask This First If the pack is close to a standard shape, a stock mould is almost always the right answer: no tooling, 1,000 pcs per colour, samples in seven days. We hold 3,000+ moulds, so 'close' is often close enough. A new mould only makes sense when the shape is the product — a custom silhouette, a multi-part assembly, a closure that does not exist. That is a capital decision, and it should be made before the quote, not after it. The bottle is the easy part; the pump is where the design is won or lost. Sanitizer sells in 50, 100, 250 and 500 ml. The 100 ml is the pocket and bag size; 250–500 ml is the counter-top and refill size. The bottle mould is usually shared with other products; the pump is not. This page covers what changes between gel and liquid, why alcohol content decides the material, and what to test before a container ships. Check it before you quote The free Bottle Spec Checker tests whether your neck fits the closure and whether the wall survives a pump stroke. 30-second check: does your bottle pass? Open ▾ Capacity (ml) Wall (mm) Closure Lotion pump Sprayer Flip-top Dropper Screw cap Full Check → — Gel Uses a Pump; Liquid Uses a Sprayer A gel sanitizer needs a pump with a wide dip tube and a larger valve, because the product does not flow on its own. A liquid sanitizer in the same bottle uses a mist sprayer with a fine orifice. The neck stays 20/410 or 24/410 either way — so a brand can launch gel and liquid from one mould, with two closures. Alcohol Content Decides the Material High-alcohol formulas (60–80 %) are the standard for sanitizer, and they are hard on some plastics over time. HDPE is the safe default; PET is fine for many formulas but should be checked for crazing at the shoulder after a few months. The practical test is a filled sample left on a shelf for four weeks, not a compatibility table. Pocket Size: 50 and 100 ml A 100 ml bottle has to survive a bag: a flip-top that opens in a handbag is the most common complaint. A screw cap with a flip spout, or a pump with a locking collar, solves it. For 50 ml travel sizes, the closure is usually the most expensive component relative to the bottle. Labels and the Sticky-Hands Problem Sanitizer bottles get handled with wet hands. Paper labels lift at the edges within weeks; a synthetic label with a waterproof adhesive, or silkscreen, survives. Silkscreen also avoids the label edge that collects residue. If the bottle is clear PET and the gel is clear, the label is the only brand surface — worth spending the extra 0.01 per unit on a better adhesive. Where Sanitizer Bottles Fail Sanitizer is handled with wet hands, in public, one-handed. Three failures. Flip-Top Opens in a Bag A 100 ml pocket bottle with a plain flip-top leaks in a handbag. A flip spout with a locking collar, or a screw cap, solves it. Alcohol and PET High-alcohol gel can craze PET at the shoulder over months. HDPE is the safe default; PET needs a four-week soak test. Pump Clogs With Gel A gel needs a pump with a wider dip tube and a larger valve. A liquid pump will stall on gel. Gel and Liquid From One Mould The neck is identical (20/410 or 24/410); only the closure changes. A brand can launch gel and liquid without a second mould, which is why sanitizer ranges often share one bottle. Do you supply the pump with the bottle? Yes, gel pumps and mist sprayers in 20/410 and 24/410, tested before packing. At 30 ml the pack decision is almost entirely about how much air the formula meets. Serums, oils and actives ship in 30 ml almost by convention. The choice that matters is the dispenser: a dropper, a standard pump, or an airless pack with a piston. This page covers what changes between the three, what it costs, and which formulas actually need the expensive option. Check it before you quote The free Bottle Spec Checker tests whether your neck fits the closure and whether the wall survives a pump stroke. 30-second check: does your bottle pass? Open ▾ Capacity (ml) Wall (mm) Closure Lotion pump Sprayer Flip-top Dropper Screw cap Full Check → — Dropper: the Default, and Its Cost A dropper is low-cost, familiar and precise enough for most oils. It is also the least protective: every time the pipette leaves the bottle, the product meets air, and the last 15–20 % of the fill is hard to draw up. For a stable oil blend in amber PET, a dropper is the right answer. For vitamin C, retinol or anything with a short shelf life after opening, it is the wrong one. Airless: Protection, at a Price An airless pack has no dip tube: a piston follows the product down, so the formula only meets air at the nozzle. Dispensing is above 95 % of the fill, and the dose is consistent from the first pump to the last. It costs 30–50 % more per unit than a dropper bottle at 30 ml, and the pack cannot be refilled. For a premium serum with an unstable active, that is usually still the lowest unit cost way to protect a expensive formula. Glass or Plastic Glass reads premium and is inert, which matters for essential oils and solvents. It is heavier, breaks, and costs more to ship. PET reads clean and modern and weighs a third as much. The dropper itself can be glass in a plastic bottle, which is the usual compromise: the pipette gives the premium feel, the bottle keeps the freight down. What to Send With the Brief Fill volume, viscosity, whether the formula contains a solvent or a strong fragrance, and the dose per use. Viscosity decides whether a dropper can draw the product at all; the solvent decides whether PET is safe over twelve months. Where Serum Bottles Fail At 30 ml the pack is mostly a dispensing decision. Three failures. Air Meets the Formula A dropper lets air in every time it leaves the bottle. For vitamin C and retinol that is the difference between six months and six weeks. Pipette Marks the Fill Level A glass pipette inserted and removed leaves product on the inside wall, so the bottle looks emptier than it is. Airless avoids it. Dropper Collar Mismatch An 18/410 collar on an 18/415 neck leaks. Confirm the thread code, not the diameter. Glass or Plastic, in Practice Glass is inert and reads premium; it is also heavier and breaks. PET is a third of the weight and cheaper to ship. The usual compromise is a glass pipette in a plastic bottle. Questions We Get on This Is 30 ml the standard serum size? Yes for face serum; 15 ml for trial and travel, 50 ml for body serum. Shampoo and conditioner are sold in 250, 300, 500 and 750 ml, almost always in HDPE or clear PET, and almost always with a pump or a flip-top. The bottle itself is simple. The failure point is the interface. We blow the bottle and mould the closure in the same building, so the pump is tested on the bottle rather than on a drawing. Open ▾ Capacity (ml) Wall (mm) Closure Lotion pump Sprayer Flip-top Dropper Screw cap Full Check → — 500 ml Is the Volume, the Neck Is the Decision A 500 ml shampoo bottle in the US is usually 24/410 with a disc-top or a lotion pump; the 750 ml family size is usually 28/410 with a heavier pump. Decoration That Survives a Bathroom Silkscreen is the default: it does not peel, and 1–4 colours cover most shampoo designs. Labels are lower in unit cost for multi-colour artwork and allow short runs; hot stamp and spray coat are for premium lines at 3,000 pcs. Avoid full-body sleeves if the bottle needs to be recyclable — the sleeve has to be removed, and most recycling lines cannot do it. Where Shampoo Bottles Fail Shampoo is the highest-volume cosmetic bottle and the most complaint-prone. Three causes. The Pump Draws Air at the End A dip tube cut to the base curve rather than pressed on it leaves 30-50 ml unusable. Customers read that as 'short fill'. The Bottle Flexes Under a Full Stroke Below 0.55 mm at the shoulder, a 500 ml PET deforms slightly with each stroke and the pump sucks air. The sign is a spongy last third. The Label Fails in the Shower Paper labels wrinkle within weeks. Synthetic label with waterproof adhesive, or silkscreen, is the only durable option in a wet bathroom. 500 ml vs 750 ml: the Economics A 750 ml needs a 28/410 pump and at least 0.65 mm at the shoulder. The bottle costs more in resin, and the pump costs more than a 24/410 — but freight per litre drops, which is why family sizes exist. For export, check the packed carton weight: a 750 ml case is heavier and can push the pallet over a weight limit that a 500 ml case does not. Text: Toner bottles — specs, MOQ and documents | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Guides / Toner bottles Guide Toner Bottles: Why 200 ml Is Replacing 250 ml, and What the Flat Shape Buys By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou · Updated 26 October 2026 Toner is the one skincare product sold by volume rather than by dose. That makes the bottle a shelf-width decision before it is a design decision — and 200 ml flat is winning that decision. Facial toner moves in 150, 200 and 250 ml. The 250 ml round bottle was the default for a decade; the 200 ml flat bottle is replacing it because it uses less shelf width and reads as a premium product rather than a bulk one. This page covers the two shapes we mould, what the flat profile changes, and the closure that suits a water-thin liquid. Check it before you quote The free Bottle Spec Checker tests whether your neck fits the closure and whether the wall survives a pump stroke. 30-second check: does your bottle pass? Open ▾ Capacity (ml) Wall (mm) Closure Lotion pump Sprayer Flip-top Dropper Screw cap Full Check → — Why Flat Beats Round on Shelf A 200 ml flat bottle presents a wide face to the shopper and takes less depth on the shelf, which lets a retailer fit one more facing in the same space. That is the entire commercial argument, and it is why the format moved. The trade-off is filling: a flat bottle needs a slightly slower line speed and a wider label area. Both are manageable at 1,000 pcs; neither is a reason to stay round. Closures for a Water-Thin Liquid Toner has almost no viscosity, so the closure decides whether the product pours or floods. A disc-top with a small orifice is the usual answer; a flip-top with a wide opening will over-pour on the first use. If the toner is applied with a cotton pad, a 20/410 neck with a controlled-flow insert is enough. If it is a mist, the bottle needs a 24/410 neck and a sprayer tested with water-thin liquid, not with water. PET or PETG Clear PET is the default: low-cost, clear, and stiff enough for a 200 ml flat profile. PETG is thicker-walled and reads more premium, at roughly 20–30 % more per unit. If the toner contains alcohol at a high percentage, check the inner compatibility before choosing PET; some alcohol levels craze the surface over months. Decoration on a Flat Face The flat face is a large print area, which makes silkscreen economical: a single colour covers most toner designs, and the flat surface prints cleanly without the distortion you get on a round bottle. Labels are also easier to apply straight on a flat face, which reduces reject rate at the co-packer. Where Toner Bottles Fail Toner is water-thin, which makes the closure the whole design. Three failures. Over-Pour on the First Use A wide flip-top floods a cotton pad. A disc-top with a 3 mm orifice, or a flow insert, fixes it. Sprayer Tested With Water A mist sprayer set for water mists coarsely with a toner. Test with the actual liquid, not water. Label on a Curved Oval An oval bottle needs a curved-surface label or a smaller flat panel; a rectangular label wrinkles at the edges. Why 200 ml Flat Replaced 250 ml Round Less shelf depth, a wider label face, and one more facing per shelf. The commercial argument is shelf geometry, not design taste. Questions We Get on This What is the standard toner bottle size? 200 ml in Asia and Europe; 250 ml in the US; 150 ml for trial sizes. Why are toner bottles flat? Less shelf depth and a larger label face; it also reads more premium than a round bulk bottle. Which closure suits toner? A disc-top with a small orifice, or a 24/410 mist sprayer tested with a water-thin liquid. Can the bottle be recycled? Clear PET recycles well. A full-body sleeve or a carbon-black cap will reduce that; specify separable parts. Is PET or PETG better? PET for cost and clarity; PETG for a thicker, more premium wall at 20–30 % more. Sections: The Three Closures That Survive a Flight; Why 50 ml Sells and 100 ml Is the Value Pack; Where Travel Bottles Fail in Practice; What to Send in a Brief; Questions We Get on This; Sizes That Fit This Guide; Get a Price on This, Within One Business Day
Text: Travel bottles — specs, MOQ and documents | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Guides / Travel bottles Guide Travel Bottles: 50 ml Is the Airline Number, and the Closure Is the Leak By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou · Updated 26 October 2026 Travel sizes are decided by a rule, not by design: 100 ml per container in hand luggage. That makes 50 ml and 100 ml the only two sizes worth moulding — and the closure the only thing that matters. Every airline regime converges on the same limit: containers of 100 ml or less, in a clear one-litre bag. So a travel range is 30, 50 and 100 ml — anything larger is not a travel bottle, it is a small bottle. The bottle is easy. The closure decides whether the product arrives at the destination. Check it before you quote The free Bottle Spec Checker tests whether your neck fits the closure and whether the wall survives a pump stroke. 30-second check: does your bottle pass? Open ▾ Capacity (ml) Wall (mm) Closure Lotion pump Sprayer Flip-top Dropper Screw cap Full Check → — The Three Closures That Survive a Flight Cabin pressure changes during a flight, and a bottle that sealed on the ground can weep in the air. Three closures handle it: a screw cap with a gasket, a flip-top with a tight spigot, and a disc-top with a silicone valve. A plain flip-top with no gasket is the one that leaks into the washbag. It is also the lowest unit cost, which is why travel sets leak. Screw Cap With Gasket The most reliable and the least convenient. Used for oils and thin liquids. Flip-Top With a Spigot A spigot that seats into the orifice holds pressure better than a flat flip lid. Check the spigot depth on the sample, not the drawing. Disc-Top With a Valve A silicone valve stops flow until squeezed, which is what a shampoo or lotion needs in a bag. Why 50 ml Sells and 100 ml Is the Value Pack 50 ml is the unit people buy for a weekend; 100 ml is the maximum allowed and reads as better value. A travel set usually pairs both: 50 ml for the carry-on, 100 ml for a longer trip. For a brand, the 50 ml is the sampler that gets a first trial, and the 100 ml is the one that gets rebought. That is why the same mould family runs both. Where Travel Bottles Fail in Practice Three failures, all testable before a container ships. Leaking at the Neck Thread A 24/415 bottle with a 24/410 cap threads on and weeps. Confirm the thread code. The Label Comes Off in the Bag Humidity plus abrasion. Synthetic label with a waterproof adhesive, or silkscreen. The Bottle Cracks in a Suitcase A 0.4 mm wall on a 100 ml survives a handbag, not a checked case. 0.5 mm is the practical floor. What to Send in a Brief Capacity, neck, closure type, and whether the pack will be sold as a set or singly. Sets need matched label positions across sizes, which is a decision made at artwork stage, not after. Questions We Get on This What is the maximum size for a travel bottle? 100 ml per container in hand luggage under most regimes; 50 ml is the common retail travel size. Which closure leaks least in a flight? A screw cap with a gasket, or a disc-top with a silicone valve. A plain flip-top is the usual culprit. Can travel bottles be refilled? Yes, and most are sold as refillable. Specify a durable thread and a valve cap. What is the MOQ? 1,000 pcs per colour on stock moulds; sets with matched labels quote per component. Less precise than injection, far cheaper for a big body. How It Works A tube of hot plastic is extruded downward, the mould closes around it and air inflates it against the walls. For a cosmetic pack that must look premium, EBM is usually the wrong process. What to Send Capacity, the closure, and whether the pack must survive a drop test filled. Injection is the process that holds a dimension, and the one that costs most per part. What We Run Closures, caps, collars, bases, droppers, thick-wall PETG bodies and every component of a multi-part assembly. Machines from small tonnage for a 20 mm cap to larger presses for a 200 mm collar. Tolerance, Honestly ±0.05 mm on a machined steel feature, ±0.1 mm on a moulded thread, ±0.15 mm on a height across a 200 mm part. Those numbers are why a seal groove is designed at 1.5–1.6 mm deep rather than "about 1.5". A blow-moulded thread moves more, which is why a bottle that must seal repeatedly is often injection moulded even though it costs more per piece. Wall and Cycle A thick wall is a slow wall: heat has to leave through the plastic, so a 2.5 mm PETG body runs a longer cycle than a 1.8 mm one. That is the real reason a thick-wall pack is expensive — not the resin alone. What to Send A drawing with the thread callout, the seal groove section and the wall. For a multi-part pack, the assembly section as well — the tolerance stack is decided here, not in the blow mould. Have an Injection Part? Send the section — we return the DFM note in 3–5 days. Why not blow-mould the thread? A blow-moulded thread moves more, so a pump that must seal repeatedly is usually on an injected neck.

Title: Injection stretch blow: neck and body | 8PCK

Text: Injection stretch blow: neck and body | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Manufacturing / Injection stretch blow Manufacturing · 02 Injection Stretch Blow: a Precise Neck, a Strong Body One process makes the preform and blows it in the same machine. The neck keeps injection tolerance; the body gains strength in two directions. Why It Exists A two-stage blow moulds the preform, cools it, then reheats and blows. One-stage does both in line: the neck stays as moulded, and the body is stretched axially and radially while still hot. That is what makes a 500 ml bottle at 20 g hold its shape with a thin wall. What It Is Good For Bottles where the neck must be exact — a pump that must not leak, a closure that must torque consistently — and the body must be light. Clear PET cosmetics, personal care, food. Where It Stops Shape freedom. A pronounced waist, a handle or a hard corner is a blow-moulding question: the parison has to reach the corner without thinning. Deep undercuts are simply not possible. What to Send Capacity, neck, weight target and a drawing or a reference bottle. If the weight matters, say what it is for — freight, feel, or a sustainability claim — because the answer changes the wall. Need a Light Bottle With a Tight Neck? Send the capacity and the closure. HDPE suits shampoo, detergent and chemicals; LDPE suits sauces and gels. Both are cheaper per gram than PET and do not shatter. Representative image — exact dimensions, colour and finish are confirmed on the approved drawing. Capacity 30–1,000 ml Material HDPE, LDPE Neck 24/410, 28/410, 38 mm Colour Natural, white, black, matched MOQ 1,000 pcs Lead time 25–35 days Not sure the neck fits your pump? Run the spec checker → Get Price in One Business Day → Download Catalogue HDPE vs LDPE HDPE is the packaging workhorse: opaque, tough, cheap, and stable with most household chemicals. LDPE is softer and used where the bottle has to be squeezed. Neither takes hot fill above about 80 °C without distortion, so for jam and sauces we quote PP. Why Polyethylene and Not PET Cost and chemical resistance. A 750 ml HDPE shampoo bottle uses less resin than the PET equivalent and does not craze with surfactants. PET wins only where clarity is the product. Recycling Note HDPE is the most widely recycled plastic after PET. Natural and white recycle best; black is invisible to near-infrared sorting, so a black HDPE bottle carries no recyclability claim. Compatibility, Packing and Tolerance Closures That Fit Send the neck finish and we match a closure from the same plant: disc-top and flip-top caps, lotion and foam pumps, mist sprayers and droppers. Closures are fitted and tested on the bottle before packing, which is where most leaks originate. Packing and Freight Carton quantity, carton dimensions and gross weight are quoted with the unit price. FOB Shantou is the default term; EXW and CIF are quoted on request. Payment is 30 % deposit, 70 % against the bill of lading. Tolerance Dimensions hold to ± 1.5 % and weight to ± 1 g against the approved drawing. Anything outside that range is remade, not discounted. Decoration Options and What They Cost in MOQ Silkscreen in one to four colours starts at 1,000 pcs and adds about five days; the plate is a one-off, which is why it does not repeat on a reorder. Labels are lower in unit cost for multi-colour artwork and allow short runs. Hot stamp, spray coat and metallising start at 3,000 pcs because the line set-up is heavier and the reject rate is higher. Decoration also decides the recycling story. A paper label with a wash-off adhesive keeps a PET bottle in the PET stream; a full-body sleeve does not. If the pack carries a recyclability claim, the decoration is part of the claim, not a design detail. Sampling and Approval A sample from an existing mould takes 7 days and comes from the production tool, not a showroom piece. For a new shape, tooling takes 15–20 days before sampling. We ship the sample with the drawing it was made to, so the approval is against a number rather than a photograph. If the formula contains alcohol, a high level of essential oil or a particulate, say so at sample stage — the compatibility test runs four weeks and it costs less to find a problem then than in a container. How We Quote and Ship Send capacity, neck, quantity and the closure you intend to use. We reply within one business day with unit price, packing data (pcs per carton, carton size, gross weight) and lead time — the packing data is what your freight forwarder needs, so it is quoted with the price rather than after. Production is 25–35 days after sample approval on existing moulds, 15–20 days longer if a new mould is needed. Payment is 30 % deposit and 70 % against the bill of lading; FOB Shantou is the default term, EXW and CIF on request. What Carbon Black Means for Black Bottles By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou Plastics News reports bans on black plastic takeout containers. The problem is not the colour — it is carbon black pigment, which sorting equipment cannot see. Black cosmetic bottles face the same issue. What Changed Plastics News reports that bans on black plastic takeout containers are spreading across US jurisdictions. The stated reason is rarely aesthetic: near-infrared sorting equipment cannot detect carbon black, so a black container falls through the recycling line and ends up in residue. What It Means for Buyers That matters well beyond takeout. Black is one of the most common cosmetic bottle colours, and it is usually produced with carbon black masterbatch. A black shampoo bottle has the same sorting problem as a black food container — the pack is invisible to the optical sorter. There are three practical routes. First, keep black and accept that the pack will not be sorted; make no recyclability claim. Second, switch to a dark colour that is detectable — deep green, brown or navy read as “black” on shelf and are visible to NIR. Third, use a detectable black masterbatch, which exists but adds cost and needs to be confirmed with the recycler rather than the pigment supplier. What to Ask a Supplier For a buyer, the question to put to a supplier is specific: is the masterbatch carbon-black based, and if so, is the pack intended for a stream that sorts it. If the answer is “it is just black”, the pack is not recyclable in most curbside systems — and a recyclability claim on the artwork will not survive a retailer audit. We mould black bottles in PET and HDPE. When a brand needs a recyclability story, we quote deep green or a detectable black instead, and say which one we are shipping. What It Changes in a Bottle Spec The Pigment Is the Problem, Not the Colour Near-infrared sorting cannot see carbon black. A black shampoo bottle has the same sorting problem as a black food container. Three Routes for a Black Pack Keep black and make no recyclability claim; switch to a deep green or brown that reads black and is detectable; or use a detectable black masterbatch, confirmed with the recycler rather than the pigment supplier. What It Means for Buyers For anyone buying bottles, that is not a policy story. It is a specification story. EPR fees are calculated on material type and weight, so the lowest unit cost bottle to buy is not always the lowest unit cost to place on a California shelf. Three numbers in your spec start to matter more than they did last year. The first is gram weight: a 500 ml PET bottle at 28 g and one at 22 g look identical and are priced differently by an EPR scheme. The second is material mix — a PET bottle with a PP cap and a full-body PVC sleeve is harder to recycle than the same bottle with a separable cap and a paper label. The third is recycled content, which some schemes reward. What to Ask a Supplier What that means in practice: ask for the bottle weight in grams, the resin, the closure material and whether the label or sleeve can be removed. None of this requires a new mould. It requires a supplier who will quote weight, not just price — and who will tell you when a thinner wall is a bad idea. What It Changes in a Bottle Spec Weight Becomes a Recurring Cost Under EPR, a heavier bottle costs more every year, not once. A 500 ml at 28 g instead of 36 g is an 8 g saving multiplied by every unit sold and every year of the fee schedule. Where Weight Can Come Off Safely The body wall, not the shoulder or base. What That Means for a Packaging Claim By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou Researchers say the evidence for enzymatic recycling of polyethylene and polypropylene is thin. For a bottle buyer, the practical lesson is simpler: design for the recycling stream that exists today. What Changed Packaging Insights reports that researchers are warning the evidence base for enzymatic recycling of PE and PP is weaker than the marketing around it suggests. What It Means for Buyers That matters to buyers because “enzymatically recyclable” has started appearing in packaging specifications, usually as a way to keep a plastic pack in a sustainability story without changing the material. There is no standard test a bottle supplier can run, no certificate that covers a finished bottle, and no collection stream that separates packaging by enzyme compatibility. What a buyer can verify today is narrower: the resin grade, the recycled content percentage, whether the pack is mono-material, and whether the label and closure can be separated. What to Ask a Supplier A practical hierarchy for a bottle spec, in order of what a retailer can actually check: mono-material PET or HDPE; a cap that separates; a label that washes off or is paper; recycled content with a declaration. It argues against putting a technology that is still in pilot into a specification that a customer will ask you to prove. The claim that survives an audit is the boring one. What It Changes in a Bottle Spec Do Not Design for a Technology That Is Not Deployed Enzymatic recycling is promising and not at scale. A mono-material PET bottle with a separable cap is recyclable today; a novel laminate justified by a future process is not. What to Ask Instead Which stream does this pack go into today, and does the cap separate without tools. Those two answers matter more than any lab result. What That Number Means for rPET By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou Plastics News reports the EU hit a 42.4% recycling rate for plastic packaging in 2024. For a bottle buyer, the number is less important than the gap between the headline rate and the rPET actually available. What Changed Plastics News reports that the EU recycled 42.4 % of plastic packaging waste in 2024. The figure is progress, and it is also the number that will be quoted at every packaging meeting for the next year. What It Means for Buyers The gap that matters to buyers is between collection and food-grade recycled material. Bottles collected curbside do not automatically become bottle-grade rPET: they have to be sorted, washed and, for food contact, run through a process that is authorised for food use. That step is where supply is tight and where the price premium lives. In practice, three things follow. First, rPET is not a commodity price: food-grade pellet can trade well above virgin PET, and the spread moves with collection rates rather than oil. Second, recycled content is a percentage on a declaration, not a marketing line, so a supplier should be able to name the grade and the percentage behind it. Third, colour matters: higher recycled content shifts clear PET slightly warmer, which is fine for amber or green packs and awkward for water-clear ones. What to Ask a Supplier For a bottle spec, the questions are short. What percentage of recycled content, which grade, is the declaration per batch or per order, and does the food-contact documentation cover the recycled input. If a supplier answers all four, the recycled claim will survive an audit. If the answer is “eco bottle”, it will not. The 42.4 % figure will rise slowly. The supply of food-grade rPET will rise more slowly still, which is why brands that lock in a grade early tend to keep it. What It Changes in a Bottle Spec Collection Is Not Food-Grade Supply The 42.4 % figure measures collection and recycling, not food-grade rPET availability. The sorting and authorisation step is the bottleneck, and the premium sits there. Four Questions on Recycled Content Percentage, grade, whether the declaration is per batch, and whether the food-contact file covers the recycled input. If a supplier cannot answer all four, the claim will not survive an audit. What Changed For anyone specifying a bottle, this is less about the bottle than about the parts attached to it. A PET bottle with a PP pump, a PP cap, a PETG collar and a PVC sleeve is four materials in one hand. The bottle was never the problem. Three changes show up in real briefs. First, caps: a PET cap on a PET bottle is now available for some neck sizes, though it costs more and limits the pump options. Second, labels: a paper label with a wash-off adhesive keeps the bottle in the PET stream; a full-body sleeve does not. The honest trade-off: a fully mono-material pack usually costs 10–20 % more and narrows the closure choice. For a brand whose recyclability claim is audited by a retailer, that is a fair trade. For a brand selling on price, a standard PET bottle with a separable cap and a paper label already meets most “design for recycling” guidelines. What to ask a supplier: which parts are which polymer, whether the cap separates without tools, whether the label washes off, and what the recycled-content percentage is. Those four answers decide whether the pack can carry a recyclability claim — not the word “mono-material” on the artwork. What It Changes in a Bottle Spec The Bottle Was Never the Problem A PET bottle with a PP pump, PP cap and PVC sleeve is four materials. Mono-material starts with the closure and the label, not the bottle. The Cost of the Claim A fully mono-material pack usually costs 10–20 % more and narrows the pump choice. That is a fair trade when a retailer audits the claim, and expensive when nobody does. Title: Packaging 2030: The Four Changes That Will Rewrite a | 8PCK
Description: Progressive Grocer maps what packaging looks like in 2030. For a bottle buyer the list is short: recycled content with proof, mono-material, EPR fees by

Text: Packaging 2030: The Four Changes That Will Rewrite a | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Trends / 2026-10-26 Outlook 2026-10-26 Packaging 2030: the Four Changes That Will Rewrite a Bottle Spec By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou Progressive Grocer maps what packaging looks like in 2030. For a bottle buyer the list is short: recycled content with proof, mono-material, EPR fees by weight, and fewer materials per pack. What Changed Progressive Grocer has published a forward look at packaging through 2030. Much of it is familiar, but four items on the list change a bottle specification rather than a marketing deck. First, recycled content with proof. The direction of travel is a declared percentage per batch, not a logo. A supplier who cannot name the grade and provide the declaration becomes a risk to the brand's claim. What It Means for Buyers Second, mono-material. Not because it is fashionable but because the sorting stream rewards it: a PET bottle with a separable cap and a paper label stays in the PET stream; a full-body sleeve does not. Third, EPR fees by weight. Under extended producer responsibility the pack's weight becomes a recurring cost, so a 500 ml bottle at 28 g instead of 36 g saves money every year, not once. That is a different payback calculation from the one most brands use. What to Ask a Supplier Fourth, fewer materials per pack. Each additional material — a metallised label, a PP collar on a PET bottle, a silicone valve — adds a line to the recyclability assessment and a fee to the EPR schedule. None of this requires a new machine. It requires deciding, at the brief stage, which of the four the pack will be judged against — and writing the spec accordingly. Text: PFAS Claims Are Moving Down the Supply Chain | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Trends / 2026-10-18 Compliance 2026-10-18 PFAS Claims Are Moving Down the Supply Chain. What Should Bottle Buyers Ask For? By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou A US water utility is suing two packaging manufacturers over alleged PFAS contamination. For buyers, the lesson is not the lawsuit — it is the paperwork you will be asked for next year. What Changed A Maine water utility has sued Huhtamaki and Sappi over alleged PFAS contamination. Whatever the outcome, the case confirms a shift that buyers have been feeling for two years: PFAS stopped being a legal question and became a purchasing question. In practice it arrives as an email from your customer — a retailer, a brand owner, sometimes your own importer — asking for a PFAS declaration before the next order ships. In the EU, the restriction proposal covers far more than food packaging. In the US, state laws are arriving one at a time, so the answer that satisfied a buyer in Ohio may not satisfy one in Minnesota. Here is where most suppliers answer badly. “We do not add PFAS” is a statement about intent, not about the article. A usable answer has two parts: a declaration from the resin supplier covering the grade actually used, and a test on the finished article — usually total organic fluorine — if the customer requires evidence rather than a statement. What It Means for Buyers Three questions worth putting in writing to any bottle supplier: 1. Can you send the PFAS statement from the resin supplier for the exact grade you will run? 2. Has the finished bottle been tested, and by which method? What to Ask a Supplier 3. Will you attach that declaration to the purchase order, so it travels with the shipment? A supplier who can answer all three in one email is worth keeping. One who answers only the first is telling you where the risk sits. Our own position is deliberately narrow: we hold ISO 9001:2015, a RoHS verification and an EU 10/2011 migration test on PE grades. PFAS-specific testing we quote per project, because it is a laboratory cost, not something we can assert. If your customer needs a document we do not have, we say so before the order — that costs less for both of us than a rejected container. What It Changes in a Bottle Spec Ask for the Declaration, Not the Assurance If PFAS are restricted in your destination market, the question to a supplier is whether the resin declaration covers them, not whether the product 'contains PFAS'. A yes/no answer is not documentation. Where PFAS Actually Appear in Packaging Rarely in the bottle. They turn up in coatings, grease-resistant liners and some release agents — which is why a bottle can be compliant while its label or liner is not. Text: The EU Is Weighing Bio-Based Targets Under PPWR | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Trends / 2026-10-28 Regulation 2026-10-28 The EU Is Weighing Bio-Based Targets Under PPWR. What It Changes for a Bottle Spec By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou Packaging Insights reports the Commission weighing bio-based plastic targets as part of the PPWR review. For a bottle buyer, the question is which claim the pack will have to prove. What Changed Packaging Insights reports the European Commission is weighing bio-based plastic packaging targets as part of the PPWR review. PPWR is the regulation that already sets recyclability and recycled-content requirements; adding a bio-based dimension changes what a bottle has to be able to prove. What It Means for Buyers The first trap is vocabulary. Bio-based, biodegradable and compostable are three different claims with three different documents. A bottle made from HDPE with 25 % straw fibre is bio-based and not biodegradable, and it recycles in the HDPE stream — a weaker claim than the word suggests, and the one that survives an audit. The second trap is accounting. Bio-based content can be measured physically (the carbon in the material) or attributed by mass balance. Both are legitimate; only one is a physical content figure, and a retailer audit will ask which is being claimed. What to Ask a Supplier The third is feedstock availability. Bio-attributed resin is chemically identical to fossil resin, which is its appeal and its risk: the supply is limited and the premium moves with the feedstock market, not with oil. For a buyer, three questions cover it: what percentage is bio-based, is it physical or mass balance, and does the pack still go into the same recycling stream. If the third answer is no, the pack has changed category and the artwork has to follow. Title: PPWR Is Already In Force | 8PCK

Text: PPWR Is Already In Force | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Trends / 2026-10-31 Compliance 2026-10-31 PPWR Is Already in Force. What Changes for a Bottle Buyer This Year? By Joe Joo · 8PCK · Shantou Regulation (EU) 2025/40 has applied since 12 August 2026. The deadlines that matter for cosmetic packaging are not the ones in the news — they are the design and labelling dates just behind them. What Changed Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste — PPWR — has applied since 12 August 2026. It replaced the old directive, which means it applies directly in every member state rather than waiting for national transposition. For a brand selling into the EU, the practical effect is that packaging is now a compliance item on the same list as the formula. The dates that matter are staggered. Minimum recyclability and design-for-recycling requirements come in later this decade, and the Commission is still working through the delegated acts that define how they are measured — including, as reported this month, rules for bioplastics. Harmonised labelling on the pack follows on its own timeline. What It Means for Buyers What that means for a bottle order placed now: the pack you design in 2026 is likely to be on shelf when the design rules bite. A mono-material PET or HDPE bottle with a compatible closure is the low-risk shape. A bottle with a metallised sleeve, a black carbon pigment or a glued-on base is the one that will need rework. Three questions worth asking a supplier before the next order. Is the body mono-material, and is the closure separable? Is the decoration compatible with the recycling stream the pack will enter — wash-off label, or direct print? And can they give you the material and additive declaration in writing, because your customer will ask for it. What to Ask a Supplier None of this requires a new mould today. It requires knowing which of your packs would fail a design review, and replacing those on the next tooling cycle rather than the one after. For an importer, the useful next step is a one-page audit per SKU: material, closure, decoration, and whether the pack can be separated by a consumer in five seconds. That is the level the rules operate at — not the chemistry of the resin, but whether the pack comes apart. We are asking the same three questions of our own range this quarter, and will publish which stock bottles pass and which need a change before the next run. The Three Questions We Ask First pH. Below 4 and above 9, the pack is a chemical decision before it is a design decision. Solvent. Material by Formula Resin Handles Avoid PET Water-based, neutral to mildly acidic, alcohol up to about 20 % Strong solvents, hot fill above ~60 °C PETG Thick-wall clarity, most emulsions, moderate alcohol Strong solvents, high heat, some essential oils HDPE Acids, alkalis, bleach, most surfactants Not for clarity; some oils permeate PP Broad chemical resistance, hot fill, closures Poor clarity, lower gloss ABS + plating Decorative caps and bases Acid peels, high alcohol, long contact with fragrance The Plated Part Is the One That Fails A champagne-gold ABS cap is a cosmetic surface over a plastic substrate. The fourth is the brand's responsibility, and any supplier who claims otherwise is guessing. What We Need to Answer Properly The formula's pH, its solvent list, the fill temperature and the expected shelf life. Not the full formula — the four lines that decide compatibility. ## https://8pck.com/packaging-engineering/part-design/
Title: Part design: wall, draft, gate and tolerance | 8PCK
Description: Wall thickness, draft, gate position and the tolerance stack on a multi-part pack.
Sections: Wall Thickness Is a Compromise, Not a Target; Draft Is Not Optional on a Visible Part; Gate Position, on a Clear Part; The Tolerance Stack: Where Four Parts Go Wrong; What to Send Us; Questions
Text: Part design: wall, draft, gate and tolerance | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Engineering / Part design Engineering · 01 Part Design: the Four Numbers That Decide Whether It Assembles Wall, draft, gate position and the tolerance stack. On a single bottle they are details; on a four-part assembly they are the difference between a product and a prototype. Wall Thickness Is a Compromise, Not a Target A thick wall looks premium and costs twice: resin per part, and cycle time per shot. On a 200 ml PETG body, moving from 2.5 mm to 1.8 mm usually keeps the shelf look and cuts the cycle by a quarter — but the shoulder becomes the weak point under a pump stroke. The rule we work to: 1.5–2.0 mm for a body under 300 ml, 0.55 mm minimum for a thin-wall bottle with a pump, and never thinner at the shoulder than at the base. If a design needs 2.5 mm for a reason we cannot see, we ask what the reason is before quoting. Draft Is Not Optional on a Visible Part Every vertical wall needs 0.5–1° of draft or the part drags on ejection and shows a scuff. On a clear bottle that scuff is visible in the shop light, which is why a "slight" draft angle is one of the most common causes of a rejected T1 sample. Gate Position, on a Clear Part The gate leaves a mark. On a transparent body it goes at the base centre or under the collar, never on the shoulder where the light hits. On a two-piece assembly the gate on the upper part is hidden by the collar, which is one reason a separate collar can be cheaper than a perfect single part. The Tolerance Stack: Where Four Parts Go Wrong Each part carries its own tolerance: ±0.1 mm on a thread, ±0.15 mm on a height, ±0.05 mm on a seal groove. On a two-part pack they add once. On a four-part assembly they add three times, and the joint that fails is usually the last one in the stack, not the one that looks weakest on a drawing. We draw the stack before the tool, and we tell you which dimension to tighten. Tightening the wrong one adds cost and fixes nothing. What to Send Us A drawing with wall, heights and the thread callout; the closure you intend to use; and the volume each chamber holds. Five lines and a sketch is enough to run the stack. Get the groove wrong and no O-ring saves it. Three Ways to Seal a Plastic Joint Type How it works Best for O-ring in a groove Elastomer compressed 15–25 % between two machined faces Reopened joints, multi-part packs Flat gasket A die-cut disc pressed on a land; needs flatness, not depth Caps, jars, wide mouths Cone or plug Two tapers meet; sealing by interference Droppers, small closures, one-time seals Most designs that "leak" use a flat gasket where an O-ring belongs: the land is too narrow, the plastic is not flat, and the seal only works on the sample that was hand-tightened. The Groove Is the Design For a 2 mm cord O-ring, the groove is typically 2.2–2.4 mm wide and 1.5–1.6 mm deep, giving 20–25 % squeeze. Too shallow and the ring is crushed and takes a set; too deep and it never touches the mating face. On a plastic part the groove also needs a radius at the edges, or the ring is cut on assembly. Material Follows Chemistry Silicone covers most emulsions and survives −40 to 200 °C. EPDM is better with solvents and worse with oils. Nitrile is the default in general industry and the wrong choice for a fragrance. We ask for the formula's solvent before we specify the ring, because changing it later means a new groove depth. The Test, Written Down "Airtight" is not a specification. The line we work to is a vacuum hold — for example −0.3 bar for 30 seconds, no bubble, no drop — plus a shake test with the real formula and a 24-hour inverted hold. If a customer has their own standard, we test to theirs. A pack that passes a vacuum test and fails a shake test is usually a thread issue, not a seal issue: the joint opens a fraction under load and the ring loses squeeze. Left-Hand Thread, and Why It Matters to a Seal If both joints on a multi-part pack turn the same way, opening the cap can unscrew the body. One side goes left-hand, so the load tightens the other joint instead of loosening it. This is a design decision, not a manufacturing one, and it has to be made before the tool is cut. Need a Joint Checked? Send the section and the formula — we return the groove and the test plan. Send a Section → We use Google Analytics to see which pages buyers actually read. No ads, no cross-site tracking. Allow Analytics No thanks QUOTE ✆ WhatsApp Get a Quote → Questions What does airtight actually mean? A defined test, not an adjective: for example −0.3 bar vacuum held for 30 seconds with no drop, plus a shake test with the real formula. O-ring or gasket? An O-ring in a groove for a reopened joint; a flat gasket needs a wide, flat land, which a blow-moulded body rarely has.

Text: Airless — 30–50 ml | 8PCK Shantou · China +86 133 6387 9944 ISO 9001 · EU 10/2011 · RoHS joe@8pck.com 8PCK EN Request a Quote Menu Home / Products / Airless 30–50 ml Airless, and Why the Last Drop Is the Whole Point Airless bottles for serum, foundation and sun care. Pump and base supplied as a set. 2 SKU Capacity All 30 50 Material All PETG Neck All Airless 30 ml Airless Bottle Airless · PETG MOQ 1,000 pcs · 30–40 days View → 50 ml Airless Bottle Airless · PETG MOQ 1,000 pcs · 30–40 days View → What Buyers Get Wrong Airless for a Water-Thin Formula A toner does not oxidise. The 30–50 % premium buys nothing the formula needs. Particles in the Piston Scrubs and glitters clog the valve; a standard pump with a wider orifice is better. Launch Quantities Under 3,000 Thick-wall PETG and a matched pump start at 3,000. At 1,000 the premium is often 2×. How an Airless Pack Works There is no dip tube. The pump sits on the product and a piston at the base rises as product leaves, so the chamber shrinks and no air enters. The formula is protected from oxidation, and the pack dispenses over 95 % of the fill against 70-80 % for a dip-tube bottle. Worth paying for when the formula is expensive or unstable (vitamin C, retinol, foundation, sun care), and not worth it for a water-thin toner or a product with large particles that clog the valve. What to Specify Before Quoting Four numbers decide the quote: capacity, dose per stroke, fill volume as a percentage, and decoration. Get those right and the pump can be matched to the viscosity without a second sampling round. Our stock moulds are 30 ml and 50 ml, both 1,000 pcs MOQ, in PETG with a PP pump. A new shape starts at 3,000-5,000 pcs. Airless vs Dropper vs Standard Pump A dropper is the least expensive way to dose a serum precisely and the least protective: the product meets air every time the pipette comes out. A standard pump bottle protects better and costs less than airless, but the dip tube leaves 20-30 % of the fill behind and the last third of the bottle dispenses unevenly. Airless costs roughly 30-50 % more per unit than a standard pump bottle at the same volume. It earns that difference when the formula oxidises, when the dose is part of the product experience, or when the claim is preservative-free. The practical test: if the product would survive six months in a dip-tube bottle, airless is a premium choice rather than a technical necessity. Decoration Changes the Price More Than the Bottle On a 30 ml airless pack, decoration often costs more than the moulded parts. A spray coat needs 3,000 pcs and adds 5-7 days; metallising needs 5,000 and adds 8-10. Silkscreen on the body is the lowest-cost option at 1,000 pcs and does not interfere with the piston chamber. If the launch quantity is under 3,000, the practical route is a clear or frosted body with a silkscreen logo, and a coloured pump collar to carry the brand colour. One more cost to plan for: an airless pack cannot be topped up at the filling line. If the fill volume is wrong, the whole batch is scrapped, so the sample must be filled with the real formula and weighed before production starts. What Buyers Get Wrong Choosing the Pouch Before the Filling Line A stand-up pouch needs a spout inserter or a top-seal sealer. If your co-packer runs bottles only, the pack changes supplier. Barrier by Assumption PET/PE is fine for dry goods; oils and aromatics need aluminium or EVOH, which then breaks the recyclability claim. Digital Printing At 10,000 Rotogravure is cheaper above roughly 20,000; digital wins below 5,000 despite the higher unit price. When a Pouch Beats a Bottle A stand-up pouch uses less plastic per litre, ships flat before filling, and takes a valve or a zipper. For refill formats and e-commerce it is usually the lower in unit cost pack, and the one that survives a courier better than a rigid bottle. The trade-off is shelf presence: a pouch stands, but it does not read as premium the way a thick-wall jar does. Most brands use both: bottle for the shelf, pouch for the refill. Material and MOQ Standard structures are PET/PE for dry and semi-liquid products, with an aluminium or EVOH layer where barrier is needed. Printing is rotogravure, which is why pouches start at 10,000 pcs rather than 1,000: the plates are the cost, not the film. Structures and When Each Is Used Stand-up pouch with a bottom gusset: the default for refills and liquids, 100 ml to 3 L, takes a spout or a valve. Three-side-seal flat pouch: samples and single servings, 5-100 ml, the lowest unit cost of the three. Kraft stand-up pouch: dry goods and coffee, with or without a window, usually with an aluminium layer for barrier. The structure decides the barrier. PET/PE is enough for dry and semi-liquid products; adding an aluminium or EVOH layer extends shelf life for oils and aromatics but makes the pouch unrecyclable in most streams, which matters if the brand is making a recyclability claim. Why the MOQ Is 10,000, Not 1,000 Pouches are printed rotogravure. Each colour needs a cylinder, and a set of cylinders costs more than the film for a small run. That is the whole reason the minimum is 10,000 rather than the 1,000 we can do on bottles: it is plates, not plastic. Digital printing is available at lower volumes at a higher unit price. Filling and Sealing A stand-up pouch needs a filling line with a spout inserter or a top-seal sealer; a three-side-seal pouch runs on a form-fill-seal machine. If your co-packer only runs bottles, the pouch moves the filling to a different supplier, which is worth knowing before the pack is chosen. Shelf life testing also changes: a pouch has a higher surface-to-volume ratio than a bottle, so barrier requirements go up quickly for oils and aromatics. If the pouch is a refill for a bottle you already sell, keep the fitment identical across both packs: a spout that does not match the bottle neck turns a refill into a complaint. Inverted Pouch: the Spout at the Wrong End An inverted pouch puts the spout at the bottom, so the product sits on it and the last portion pours without tilting. It is the standard pack for sauces, pastes and refill concentrates — and for anything a customer uses one-handed. The cost is in the fitment, not the film: an inverted spout needs a heavier valve and a wider base seal, which adds roughly 15-20 % to the bag cost at 10,000 pcs.
